question: A 70-year-old woman presents with bilateral knee pain for 3 years, worse on climbing stairs, with morning stiffness lasting 10 minutes. Knee X-ray report: 'joint space narrowing medial compartment, subchondral sclerosis, osteophytes at femoral condyle and tibial plateau — features of osteoarthritis.' She asks why her knees hurt so much when the report says 'just arthritis.' Which clinico-radiological correlation BEST explains her symptoms?

answers.text: The X-ray findings directly measure pain; severe narrowing means severe pain, and her symptoms are therefore proportionate.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Radiographic severity and symptom severity are weakly correlated in osteoarthritis. Many patients with severe X-ray changes have minimal pain; others with early changes are severely disabled. This is a core clinico-radiological correlation principle.

answers.text: The X-ray shows late structural damage (cartilage loss → joint space narrowing; bone remodelling → sclerosis and osteophytes), but pain arises from synovitis, subchondral bone stress, periarticular muscle fatigue, and central sensitisation — processes largely invisible on plain film.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. This is the gold-standard explanation: X-ray reflects structural pathology, not pain generators. Synovitis, subchondral stress, neuromuscular fatigue, and central sensitisation drive symptoms. Treating her imaging, not her patient, would be the clinical error.

answers.text: The radiologist has under-reported the findings; request an MRI to find the true cause of her pain.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The X-ray report is appropriate for osteoarthritis. MRI would show cartilage and marrow changes more clearly but would not change the fundamental clinico-radiological mismatch. The solution is correlation, not additional imaging.

answers.text: Short morning stiffness (<30 min) distinguishes osteoarthritis from rheumatoid arthritis, so no correlation with imaging is needed — the diagnosis is clinical.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Short morning stiffness does support OA over RA, but clinico-radiological correlation is still needed to explain her symptoms to her and to guide management. Recognising that X-ray severity does not equal symptom severity is essential clinical communication.

overallFeedback.feedback: The key principle: X-ray reflects structural pathology, not pain. In OA, radiographic severity (joint space narrowing, sclerosis, osteophytes) predicts structural damage, not symptom burden. Pain generators (synovitis, subchondral stress, central sensitisation) are largely invisible on plain film.

Excellent. Clinico-radiological correlation means reading the imaging against anatomy, pathophysiology, and the patient's presentation — recognising that structural damage visible on X-ray and functional disability experienced by the patient can diverge substantially.
